Solomon Islands ends controversial security pact with China for Australian treaty

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Australia and the Solomon Islands have signed a latest treaty on security and economics.
  • The Solomon Islands has signed a "historic" treaty with Australia, after reportedly telling China it was ending a controversial security pact signed in 2022.
  • At a press conference in Canberra on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the new treaty would ensure that Australia was the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Australia and the Solomon Islands have signed a latest treaty on security and economics.

The Solomon Islands has signed a "historic" treaty with Australia, after reportedly telling China it was ending a controversial security pact signed in 2022.

At a press conference in Canberra on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the new treaty would ensure that Australia was the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice".

In 2022 the Solomon Islands, then under the leadership of now-Opposition Leader Manasseh Sogavare, signed a security and policing pact with Beijing.

There were fears the pact gave China a crucial military and strategic foothold in the Pacific amid a battle for influence in the region with the US.

On Tuesday, Australian media outlets reported that Honiara had told Beijing it would not renew the pact, understood to be expiring in April 2027.

Wale told reporters on Wednesday there were "ongoing discussions" with China but he was "unable to talk about" the pact, because of a non-disclosure agreement.

He remarked the treaty with Australia provided a reset after several years in which the Solomon Islands had been a point of "uncertainty and doubt in the region".

"Those days are done, gone," Wale stated.

Albanese said the treaty would strengthen the two countries' security partnership.

"Backing our Pacific neighbours is an investment in Australia's own security and our own prosperity.".

"We'll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions.".

On Tuesday China's foreign ministry spokesman, Guo Jiukan, did not confirm or deny that the pact had been terminated.

"There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and Pacific island countries, including the Solomon Islands," Guo remarked.

The pact was never publicly released, but leaked excerpts revealed it gave China extensive involvement in security and policing including deploying its own officers to the Solomon Islands, and allowed it to establish a quasi military base.

It was a "massive coup" for Beijing, mentioned Lowy Institute Research Fellow, Dr Connor Graham, but its unprecedented scale sparked alarm in the Pacific and the West.

Wednesday's treaty had delivered "an enormous win for Canberra", and "closes the loop" on a series of security deals Canberra signed with Pacific nations in the wake of the Solomons-China pact.

"That [China pact] was the thing that put fear in the hearts of diplomats in Washington and Canberra," he told the BBC.

William Yang, the International Crisis Group's Senior Analyst for North East Asia, mentioned the end of China's "flagship" Pacific deal and the signing of the upcoming treaty also reaffirmed the Pacific's "longstanding consensus-based decision-making model, especially in the security space".

It has been revealed that under the new treaty, the Solomon Islands commits to prior consultation with Australia on critical infrastructure and to ensure any security cooperations are with Pacific Islands Forum members. China is a dialogue partner but not a member of the forum.

Honiara also commits to its sensitive infrastructure remaining "free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access", and to not permit its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base.

The Solomons will receive support for its free education system and sports programs, improved visa arrangements, and support for the expansion of affordable and renewable energy and infrastructure development.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this week the ABC reported the package promised more than A$980m (Â£460.7m, $648,000) in additional funding, citing leaked text messages. The BBC has not independently verified the text messages.

According to recent reports, wale visited Australia to sign the treaty, accompanied by two dozen Solomons MPs. He and Albanese said the size of the delegation demonstrated that the treaty had strong support from the country's parliament, after years of political instability - largely driven by disagreement over the country's relationship with China.

South Africa's Ramaphosa wins court battle over impeachment threat

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Cyril Ramaphosa has faced calls to resign over his handling of the "Farmgate" scandal.
  • South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal battle to overturn a report that found he may have a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.
  • In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (Â£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Cyril Ramaphosa has faced calls to resign over his handling of the "Farmgate" scandal.

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal battle to overturn a report that found he may have a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.

In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (Â£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. He denied any wrongdoing.

Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report in court after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him.

The Western Cape high court ruled that the panel's report was unlawful and set it aside "in its entirety".

In its judgment, the court said the panel, appointed by parliament to investigate the allegations against Ramaphosa, had "misconstrued its function, the nature of the inquiry it was to conduct and the recommendation it was required to make".

Sources indicate that "It went beyond its lawful remit ... and made several material errors of law. [Therefore] the report of the independent panel ... is declared unlawful and is reviewed and set aside in its entirety," Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana mentioned.

The court also declared unlawful the steps taken by parliament in relation to the report.

Political analyst Khanyi Magubane remarked the court ruling was a victory for Ramaphosa as it gave him "political and constitutional credibility".

She made it clear that the ruling was not a criminal finding on possible improper conduct at the farm but rather an indictment at the independent panel's report.

Sources indicate that "[So] he does get significant reprieve ... but there will always be the shadow of the Phala Phala report," Magubane said.

The ruling effectively removes the basis for the parliamentary impeachment process against Ramaphosa, although opposition parties have indicated they intend to challenge the decision.

The scandal, dubbed "Farmgate" by local media, has has dogged Ramaphosa since it emerged in 2022, when former spy chief Arthur Fraser reported the matter to police in a dossier.

Fraser, an ally of former President Jacob Zuma, accused Ramaphosa of concealing the theft from the police and tax authorities.

The break-in took place in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.

Opposition parties, pictured above, have been vocal in their call for the president to account for his role in the saga.

Earlier this month, two people were found guilty of the theft.

Ramaphosa confirmed that a robbery had taken place but noted the money had been from the legitimate sale of buffalo from his livestock business.

Several investigations cleared him of any wrongdoing, but parliament began an impeachment proceedings in 2022 and appointed an independent panel to investigate the allegations.

The panel made a series of damaging findings, including that there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen".

It also concluded that Ramaphosa "has a case to answer".

Ramaphosa initially challenged the report in court but withdrew his application after parliament voted against adopting its findings.

He revived the legal challenge again in May this year after the Constitutional Court, the country's highest court, ruled that parliament had acted unconstitutionally by blocking moves to impeach him.

It ordered parliament to refer the report to an impeachment committee.

In his latest challenge, Ramaphosa argued that the panel had "misconceived its mandate, misjudged the information placed before it and misinterpreted the four charges advanced against me".

The Western Cape High Court's ruling could bring the current impeachment process to an end, unless parliament successfully challenges the decision.

If they do, and the appeal is successful, the parliamentary committee would be able to examine the charges against the president and make a recommendation.

If the committee recommends impeachment, parliament would have to vote on whether to remove him from office. This would require the support of at least two-thirds majority in parliament.

Ramaphosa's Africa National Congress (ANC) has enough parliamentary seats to block such a move.

He is the first president to face impeachment proceedings under the rules introduced in 2018.

Legal expert Professor Richard Calland told the BBC he had expected the court ruling, given what he termed as "fault lines" in the independent panel's report.

Calland stated the court's findings now meant that the impeachment process was "dead in the water [and] cannot continue".

He said that any political party that wanted to revive it "would have to come up with a whole new basis" for this.

Calland stated political parties who want to hold Ramaphosa accountable would likely seek to appeal the ruling but it was unlikely parliament would also do so.

"So, the president's political career is now free of the cloud of impeachment," he said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi on Tuesday, the US Coast Guard notes.

Recent findings suggest that the Cessna 210 was on its way from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware. Air traffic control lost touch with it at about 15:45 (21:45 GMT) and it later went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula and Horn Island, officials said.

Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, noted Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.

Rescuers spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, he stated.

Cmdr Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard rescue mission co-ordinator, noted: "While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency co-ordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has declared.
  • Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pete Edochie was one of Africa's most celebrated film stars.

Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has declared.

Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs.

In a statement, his family mentioned Edochie died in the early hours of Wednesday in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

Tributes are pouring in from fans and fellow actors, remembering him as a Nollywood legend who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.

Edochie began his career as a broadcaster in 1967 before turning to acting. He rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.

His portrayal of Okonkwo, the proud but troubled Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart, earned him international recognition helping establish him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors.

The television series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.

He went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has since grown into one of the world's largest film industries.

Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire's Club and the 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart.

His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).

He also received several other accolades during his career, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.

In recent years, his distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films found a new generation of admirers through viral social media memes.

"As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss," a statement shared on Instagram by his son Leo stated.

Enugu State Governor Peter Mbah mentioned Edochie's death was a huge loss to Nigeria, praising the actor for introducing international audiences to Igbo traditions and inspiring younger performers.

"Pete Edochie was more than an accomplished actor, he was an institution," Mbah said.

The Actors Guild of Nigeria (AGN) president, Abubakar Yakubu, described Edochie as a "father figure" in the entertainment industry, saying his influence would be felt for generations to come.

Edochie had spoken publicly about his deteriorating health during a visit to Ghana in October, saying he was struggling to walk and experiencing swelling in parts of his body.

He is survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including fellow Nollywood actors Yul and Linc Edochie.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Relatives of those being held hostage spent anxious hours as the situation unfolded.

Colombian security forces have freed around 20 shoppers and employees who had been held hostage for about 17 hours at a supermarket in the city of Cartagena.

Gunmen had stormed into the building at 08:00 local time (13:00 GMT) on Tuesday after what Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella stated was a failed attempt at robbing an armoured car carrying money.

They held those inside at gunpoint while trying to negotiate their getaway.

With the situation becoming ever more intense as the day progressed, de la Espriella gave the green light for special forces and police to launch a daring operation to free the hostages, killing one gunman.

Residents living near the supermarket reported hearing explosions as the security forces moved into the building.

Industry observers note that police later confirmed that officers had used stun grenades to overpower the hostage-takers. Four have been arrested.

Around 20 people were still being held hostage when the security forces moved in.

De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he noted had been carried out "flawlessly".

He flew into the northern city to oversee the operation personally. He could be seen flanked by the commanders of the operation with a handgun strapped to his belt, in footage released following its conclusion.

De la Espriella mentioned the gunmen had been given the chance to hand themselves in but had refused.

Earlier in the day, the assailants had freed 10 of the hostages, among them elderly women.

But they continued to hold around 20, even as a police helicopter hovered above and special forces teams prepared to enter the building, located in a popular shopping centre.

Local media report that, as well as asking for safe passage out of the supermarket, the gunmen also demanded nearly $2m (Â£1.5m) and armoured vehicles.

De la Espriella said they had no political affiliations but had taken the hostages once their blueprint to rob a cash-laden armoured car had been foiled.

"It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping - no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out and then kidnapped a group of people," he noted.

Johan Correa, one of the rescued hostages, described to local media how the gunmen, who he said had been disguised, had entered the supermarket, where he worked.

"We had just started our shift when some guys dressed as police officers came in and started robbing the place," he said. "They were robbers, but we thought they were police.".

He added that he and other hostages had been locked in a cold storage room, face down with their hands tied.

"We were there for more than four hours, lying on the floor with our hands tied, and it was a really tough experience.".

Another employee, Dayro Rafael VelÃ¡zquez Castrillo, told Caracol radio that the assailants wore masks and had been armed with guns and knives.

VelÃ¡zquez stated the gunmen repeatedly threatened the hostages, telling them that they had rigged the exits with explosives.

Relatives and bystanders congregated outside the entrance to the supermarket.

He noted that "thank God" they had been rescued, describing moments of tension as they heard explosions and a helicopter flying above.

Photos taken during the rescue operation show armed soldiers inside the building as people kneel with their hands behind their heads.

It is unclear from the photos whether those kneeling are hostages or the hostage-takers.

Local media report that the authorities feared that some of the gunmen may have tried to pass themselves off as hostages as the rescue mission unfolded.

The identities of the four arrested have not yet been released.

The hostages are being reunited with their families after being checked over by medical teams, according to the mayor of Cartagena.

Many anxious relatives had spent hours waiting for news outside the perimeter place around the supermarket by security forces.

A woman called Sandra told Caracol that her 76-year-old mother was one of those being held hostage.

Sandra's mother - among a group of elderly people released after six hours - was reunited with her daughters and grandchildren.

Footage recorded by local media showed bystanders cheering as some of those freed were escorted to ambulances waiting nearby.

But with around 20 people still inside the building, tension outside rose and police stated they had to stop some of the relatives from breaching the perimeter.

At one point, flights into the city were halted, with planes diverted to Barranquilla.

Special forces, including units specialised in dealing with kidnappings, were deployed to Cartagena, a popular destination among foreign and Colombian tourists.

Cartagena's Mayor Dumek Turbay called for calm but the granddaughter of one of the hostages told Colombian newspaper El Tiempo that "this shows we're not safe anywhere".

De la Espriella was elected earlier this year on a promise to crack down on Colombia's criminal groups.

He had travelled to the central city of Villavicencio to inspect the damage caused by a car bomb that detonated outside the regional government's offices on Tuesday.

While de la Espriella blamed the leader of a dissident rebel group for that attack, he was adamant that the hostage takers were "simple bandits" without political affiliations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex has been charged by a federal grand jury in Los Angeles with possessing child sex abuse images.

Markle, who remains in custody in Florida, allegedly possessed materials that include at least one image involving a prepubescent minor and a minor under 12 years old, court documents filed in California show.

The 82-year-old has denied possessing images of child sex abuse.

Last week, a judge in Florida declared Prince Harry's father-in-law mentally competent to stand trial.

Industry observers note that the FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home in Florida on a single federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material. He now faces two counts.

US attorney Bill Essayli stated Markle faces a maximum of 20 years in prison on each count if convicted.

His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles for almost two decades uncovered the abuse material.

Markle was initially released on conditional bail but was then ordered to stay in jail pending trial after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.

Watch: Thomas Markle's charges over child sexual abuse material.

In the indictment, filed by the US Attorney's Office in the Central District of California, Markle is accused of knowingly possessing 35mm film negatives on 30 October and 4 November that contained child sexual abuse materials.

The US Attorney's Office said that during both instances Markle allegedly knew the images contained such materials.

Inside the storage units, federal agents found two images that depict an adult man - whom a witness identified as Markle - with an underage child, the US attorney's office said.

They also alleged that a third image appears to depict a child in a room believed to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and he lived in Cebu until May.

"The affidavit also describes additional photographs that appear to show Markle with children in various stages of undress," prosecutors mentioned.

Judge finds Thomas Markle mentally fit to stand trial on child abuse charges.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Russian MiG-31 military jet (file photo).

Ukraine has said it damaged five Russian military aircraft in an attack on Russia's Savasleyka airfield, 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow.

Sources indicate that three MiG-31 and two Su-34s aircraft were hit, Kyiv's General Staff stated, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed but that "there may be even better news to come". It did not elaborate on what weapons it had used to hit the airfield.

Russia has not commented on the strikes.

Sources indicate that the airfield at Savasleyka, in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, has been a target for Ukraine for several years. It hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs.

The take-off of MiG-31s in particular frequently triggers nationwide alerts across Ukraine, as the Kinzhal missiles they carry have been known to hit large infrastructure and military targets and are difficult to shoot down.

Overnight, Kyiv also said it hit two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region some 800km (500 miles) from the front line â the latest in a series of long-range strikes which have dented Moscow's oil processing capacity.

"Did you repair them? We'll hit them again," the defence ministry in Kyiv noted.

Samara region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev remarked the night-time attacks had been "a true ordeal", with more than 145 drones shot down. One person was killed and several towns experienced power outages, Fedorishchev said.

Kyiv also stated it had hit a radar system as well as fuel and logistics depots across Ukrainian territories currently occupied by Russia.

"Without fuel, military vehicles cannot move; without ammunition, artillery falls silent," the defence ministry noted, adding that every successful hit meant Moscow could carry out fewer strikes.

Kyiv has developed a thriving weapons industry and Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets well beyond the front line have become commonplace in the years since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.

On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin called for a tightening of security measures across the country's energy facilities.

But he also argued that Russia had managed to stabilise its domestic fuel market without suffering "critical damage" and added that Moscow would "inevitably" retaliate against Kyiv.

Ukraine continues to come under daily attack. Ten people were killed across several regions between 24 and 25 November, while thousands are without power after Russian strikes on energy infrastructure.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

Close-up images to be revealed of asteroid deliberately hit to test ability to protect Earth

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Hera spacecraft will study the 150m-wide (490ft) asteroid called Dimorphos.
  • Pictures will be released later of damage to an asteroid that was deliberately hit with a spacecraft four years ago as part of a test of Earth's defences.
  • In what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it slightly off course.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Hera spacecraft will study the 150m-wide (490ft) asteroid called Dimorphos.

Pictures will be released later of damage to an asteroid that was deliberately hit with a spacecraft four years ago as part of a test of Earth's defences.

In what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it slightly off course.

The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Now, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday.

The asteroid poses no threat. Instead, this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock were heading for our planet.

"Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.

This was the last image from Dart before it crashed into Dimorphos in 2022.

The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m wide.

Sources indicate that the Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km/h (14,000mph). Images beamed back demonstrated the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out upon impact.

It was such a major smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.

The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.

Before the collision, it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the Dart crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.

But the arrival of the second spacecraft, Hera, will help scientists answer many more questions.

"Dart exploded in the asteroid and therefore we don't have the information of what is its final state," explained Michel.

Industry observers note that "The impact could have left a crater - and if it is the case, we need to understand the size and the depth. Or [the impact] may have entirely reshaped the asteroid.".

A 10,000km-long (6,200 miles) debris trail was spotted by the Hubble Space Telescope.

The Hera mission will spend the next year studying Dimorphos and will look at Didymos too.

The spacecraft is packed with instruments and has two small shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid.

A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.

This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.

"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," remarked Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.

"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'.".

Hera has already sent back an image of Didymos with Dimorphos in the background.

Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet.

Industry observers note that the biggest, which measure more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city.

"We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," noted Carolyn Ernst, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who works on both the Dart and Hera missions.

Recent findings suggest that "The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there.".

She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted and none are heading to Earth.

"The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added.

In a recent development, "But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that.".

Hera has two small satellites onboard to study the asteroid up close.

Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks - to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us.

A latest mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids: a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor.

There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including one called Apophis, which is about 450m long.

Apophis was discovered in 2004 and was initially thought to have the potential to hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029.

Industry observers note that but now scientists understand its orbit better and say it will not hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km above our surface.

This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close.

Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).

Nasa's Dart spacecraft 'changed path of asteroid'.

#148. Breaking: My family were killed in Ukraine. My mum blamed Zelensky's troops - the truth is complicated

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2164 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: My family were killed in Ukraine. My mum blamed Zelensky's troops - the truth is complicated

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2164 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Watch: BBC reporter investigates deaths of family members in Russia-Ukraine war.
  • Sources indicate that I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine.
  • In a recent development, the woman who sent me the photo indicates the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watch: BBC reporter investigates deaths of family members in Russia-Ukraine war.

Sources indicate that I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering.

In a recent development, the woman who sent me the photo indicates the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse.

The photo Anastasiya was sent of her grandparents' graves.

I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message.

"Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it remarked.

It turned my world upside down.

Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life.

Mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict.

Anastasiya (bottom left) with her father (top left) and grandparents (right) before the war.

Backing Moscow is not that unusual in the Donbas region - the predominantly Russian-speaking part of eastern Ukraine where my village Dachne is located.

After pro-Russian forces captured large parts of the Donbas in 2014, many of those who stayed supported Moscow over Kyiv, a stance cemented by exposure to Russian state TV.

Industry observers note that now the Russians occupy almost 80% of Donetsk - the part of the Donbas where my village is. Over the past nearly five years, since Russia's full-scale invasion, entire towns and cities have been razed to the ground, external.

The remains of Anastasiya's family home are circled in a frame of a video, filmed by Ukraine's 33rd Mechanised Brigade on 27 January 2025.

I had already fallen out with my sister Sasha, who had been living in Moscow with her young family when the war broke out. She refused to take sides - I felt hurt and cut her off.

But earlier this year, around the first anniversary of dad's death, Sasha unexpectedly texted me. We started talking over text about our childhood - the way things used to be. I realised I was not angry with her anymore. She too was grieving, missing dad just as much as I was.

Anastasiya's father Serezha - he stayed in Dachne to look after his elderly parents.

In a recent development, I told her I wanted to make a documentary about dad and she was very supportive. I knew then that I had an ally on my journey. But we decided not to tell our mum just yet.

In a recent development, I started looking for witnesses to the events in Dachne that took place in January 2025, the month dad is believed to have been killed. It was not easy. It was a village of a few hundred people, but many had left, others had died, and those who remained had limited phone signals.

Russia publicly declared the capture of Dachne on 14 February and it has remained under Moscow's control ever since.

This meant it was impossible for me to travel there in person. So I began trying to contact my family's neighbours.

Anastasiya could not safely travel back to Dachne, so she worked through contacts in village group chats.

In a Dachne village messaging chat, I found the number of a man I'll call Misha. I was told he had been with my father on the day he died. Speaking to the BBC could put him in danger with the Russian occupiers, so I did not tell him I worked for the BBC or that I was recording our call.

According to recent reports, misha told me that on 26 January he had looked in on my father and realised he had been injured. Serezha told him he had been "clipped" by a drone, and had asked Misha to bring a first aid kit, he stated.

It is impossible to know which side was operating the drone that killed my father, but we do know that Russian drones were constantly targeting the village at that time.

"I asked if the wound was serious. He [Serezha] noted it wasn't," said Misha - but then recalling how, when he had returned to check on my father a couple of hours later, he had found him dead.

With the help of two other villagers, Misha noted they had buried him in the greenhouse.

"I'm sorry I couldn't save him," Misha told me.

BBC Eye Investigations: Who Killed My Family?

BBC journalist Anastasiya Gribanova investigates who killed her father and grandparents in Ukraine, uncovering painful accounts as she tries to reunite her divided family.

Watch on BBC iPlayer or listen on BBC Sounds now (UK only).

If you are outside of the UK, listen to the Who Killed My Family podcast here.

Watch our YouTube documentary here, external.

As for my grandparents, my investigations suggested the events surrounding their deaths may have been more complicated.

Industry observers note that their house, on the eastern side of Dachne, had been destroyed. Neighbours told me they had escaped to another home on the same street.

I eventually reached a woman I'll call Lina, who lived nearby and was the last person, as far as I know, who saw my grandparents alive.

She could not recall what this date was, but knew it was in the second half of January.

At this time, she said, "the Russians were fully advancing - the edges of the village were being shelled. Then the Ukrainian soldiers moved from the edge of the village into the centre. They hid in people's yards and used side streets to avoid drones.".

In a recent development, she noted two soldiers entered her property. They had not been wearing any identifying insignia but had been speaking Ukrainian, she said - a language that Lina described as "Bandera", a derogatory term for Ukrainians.

According to recent reports, "You're going to have to leave. Why are you still here?" Lina mentioned they had asked her.

She remarked one had pointed a machine gun at her as she had stood outside her house, while another had gone to see my grandparents. She told me she had feared for her life and then fled her house for the night.

The following day, she told me she had returned to my grandparents' street to check on them.

She had found the door to the house they had been staying in open, she mentioned, despite the freezing conditions.

According to recent reports, with drones buzzing overhead, Lina said she had not dared look inside, but had later heard from neighbours that my grandparents had been found dead. She believed it had been the Ukrainian soldiers who visited her house who had shot them.

Another neighbour, who I will call Maria, described discovering their bodies - my grandmother in bed, covered in a blanket, and my grandfather lying on the floor in a pool of now-dried blood.

Maria also believed Ukrainian soldiers had killed them - because, she remarked, that she too had felt threatened by Ukrainian troops at the time.

"If they had seen me they would have killed me too.".

Her theory was that my grandparents had irritated the troops in some way.

According to recent reports, "Your grandparents caught them in a bad mood because your grandfather was always asking to be evacuated. And [the soldiers] were, you know, high. They were taking drugs. So your grandparents got in their way," she told me.

Most of the other people in the village I spoke to also believe Ukrainian soldiers killed them, though their testimony is not based on direct evidence.

The latest local mayor, appointed by the Russian occupiers when they finally took control of Dachne in February, mentioned she had been present at my grandparents' burial the following month, and said half of my grandmother's skull was missing.

These accounts of how they might have died in January 2025 were deeply disturbing, though no-one had witnessed their deaths and the information I was given could not be independently verified.

The villagers I spoke to - now living in occupied territory - did say there had been some tensions between themselves and Ukrainian troops at the time, because the soldiers had viewed those who remained in Dachne as supporters of Russia.

The clinical causes of my grandparents' deaths are unclear.

Their bodies were not exhumed for nearly 20 months, when the local authorities sent them to a morgue in the occupied region, where a basic autopsy was carried out by a forensics expert.

He told me that my grandmother had died of an explosives injury to the skull - but could not specify its cause.

As for my grandfather, it said his body had shown no obvious signs of injury.

I compared two satellite images of the house in which their bodies were found - from just before and just after when they are believed to have died - and could detect no significant damage to the building in the second image.

I also spoke to a villager who mentioned he had buried my grandparents.

He remarked he did not know anything about who killed them.

It has been revealed that "I wasn't there. But why would you kill old people?" he asked.

Anastasiya does not know if she will ever be able to give her grandparents (pictured) a dignified burial.

Recent findings suggest that I examined military maps from DeepStateMap.Live, an open-source Ukrainian resource, and US think tank Institute for the Study of War. They suggested Ukrainian forces still held the street where my grandparents lived during the week they had died, although the front line had been shifting rapidly.

Industry observers note that my colleagues helped me identify the Russian military units that went on to capture Dachne. We found telephone numbers of Russian soldiers. But none of them agreed to speak to me.

I turned to the Ukrainian military.

A soldier from the 33rd Mechanised Brigade, who gave his name simply as Vlad, stated his unit had still been in Dachne at the time my grandparents were believed to have died and that the Russians had been swiftly advancing.

Another Ukrainian soldier I spoke to also confirmed Ukraine's troops had still been in control of some parts of Dachne in late January.

We put our findings on the deaths of my grandparents to the Ukrainian military.

It said it had no verified evidence on how they died, or which implicated its servicemen during the "intense hostilities". It added that investigating allegations of wrongdoing was the role of law enforcement.

We also approached Russia's ministry of defence and Russia's embassy in London for comment - they did not respond.

Sisters Sasha (right) and Anastasiya were reunited at Belgrade Airport.

The Donetsk regional prosecutor's office, which is now based outside Russian-controlled territory, has documented alleged Russian war crimes reported by eyewitnesses in villages around Dachne during December 2024 and January 2025 - including the killing of five civilians in a basement in the nearby village of Kostyantynopilske.

Recent findings suggest that however, Ukrainian investigators have no equivalent cases registered in Dachne during that period. They have documented only three deaths there. My father and grandparents are not among them.

Their bodies lie in occupied territory, and I do not know if I will ever be able to say goodbye properly and bury them with dignity.

There is little more I can do for them, except one thing - mend my relationship with my sister and my mother.

Almost three years after I last saw my sister, I fly to Belgrade where she now lives.

Anastasiya (left) and her sister Sasha look through photos of their father.

In a recent development, she is waiting for me at the airport, holding lilies, and a plate with a silly nickname on it that she gave me when we were children. We hug, cry and laugh. It feels as if something between us is finally falling back into place.

At her flat, we look through family photographs and talk about my investigation and what I was able to find. My grief is still there, but it hurts a little less. I'm no longer carrying it alone.

"Are you ready?" Sasha asks. She rings our mother - who has also moved to Serbia - and puts the phone on speaker.

"Hi, Mum. It's Nastya," I say. First there is silence. Then I hear her crying. "Nastya, my darling, hello," she replies.
